With the aim of informing the selection of biomass pretreatment options and to assist in interpreting experimental results from different biomass/solvent combinations, this study addresses the impact of crystallinity and size on the kinetics of semicrystalline cellulose fiber swelling and dissolution. To this end, a newly developed phenomenological model is utilized that accounts for the role of decrystallization and disentanglement as two rate-determinant steps in the cellulose dissolution process. Although fibers with lower crystallinity swell more and faster, the degree of crystallinity does not affect the dissolution rate. Fibers of smaller diameter swell more and become amorphous faster. When decrystallization is important, the solubility of thinner fibers increases more with a reduction in the crystallinity compared to the diameter. However, when the dissolution is controlled by chain disentanglement, or in the case of dissolution of fibers having larger diameters, milling the fibers to reduce the particle size could increase the solubility. fetched_contents.text: Comparison of various milling modes combined to the enzymatic hydrolysis of lignocellulosic biomass for bioenergy production: Glucose yield and energy efficiency Highlights * • VBM (vibro ball milling) was the most effective in decreasing of cellulose crystallinity. * • BM (ball milling) was the most effective in increasing surface area. * • The highest energy efficiency was obtained with CM (centrifugal milling). Abstract Bagasse is an abundant by-product from sugarcane production that can be used for conversion into biofuels. Nonetheless, the recalcitrant structures of lignocellulosic fibers required a pretreatment prior conversion into biofuels. In this study, four mechanical deconstruction methods were compared in terms of energy demand and energy efficiency at lab scale: BM (ball mill), VBM (vibratory ball mill), CM (centrifugal mill) and JM (jet mill). Results indicate that VBM was more effective compared to BM, JM and CM in enzymatic accessibility and sugars solubilization: VBM-3h > BM-72 h > JM-5000 rpm > CM-0.12 mm. However, preliminary energetic assessment showed that at lab scale, the CM (centrifugal mill) as mechanical fractionation process appears to be the most efficient in terms of energy-efficiency (kg glucose/kWh) compared to BM, VBM and JM. A comparison with literature pretreatments data highlighted that fine and/or ultrafine milling process (BM, VBM, CM) are simpler saccharification technologies, which not required any chemical or water inputs, thus minimizing waste generation and treatment. Introduction In the future, petroleum refineries will be substituted by biorefineries, where wastes will be cracked into oil, synthons, bioenergy or biomaterials [1]. Many crops, agro-resources, or agro-industrial wastes are used for this reason. Among them, sugar cane is an ideal plant to serve as a basis for biorefining [2], [3]. Indeed, sugarcane produces sugars and several molecules of high added value [4], but also BG (bagasse), which is a lignocellulosic biomass, with an amount of 279 MMT (million metric tons) generated annually on a global level [5]. BG is a fibrous residue, which consists mainly of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin. Enzymatic hydrolysis of the main components of the sugarcane bagasse is one of the promising methods to further upgrading it into biofuels [6]. The enzymatic hydrolysis can be influenced by various physicochemical parameters like accessible surface area, cellulose crystallinity, lignin content and distribution, hemicelluloses structure and lignin–hemicelluloses–cellulose association [6], [7], [8], [9]. A pretreatment process is therefore recommended in order to: i) modify the structure and architecture of the lignocellulose, ii) reduce particles size and cellulose crystallinity, and iii) increase the accessible surface area and porosity [10], [11], [12]. A number of pretreatment methods have been developed to improve the conversion of sugars polymers (i.e. cellulose, hemicellulose) into fermentable sugars aiming to maximize biofuels production [9], [11], [13]. Pretreatment technologies include mechanical, chemical, physicochemical and biological methods or a combination of these techniques [10]. Most of lignocellulosic biomass pretreatments are currently based on the use of expensive chemical processes multistep, which, in some cases, consume large amount of water and chemical quantities and generate significant wastes (i.e. effluents). Low or no water consumption during lignocellulosic pretreatment can decrease the effluents, and also reduce the energy input for the biomass pretreatment [9], [10], [14], [15]. For this purpose, mechanical fractionation of lignocellulosic biomass could be one promising alternative for a sustainable future dry biorefinery with low water and chemical consumption and thus low waste production. In recent years, the development of environmentally friendly pretreatment such as milling, ultrasonic, plasma and wet explosion has been studied with woods, bagasse, rice and wheat straw [14], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21]. Mechanical fractionation of biomass by hammer mills, knife mills, disk mills, ball mills, vibratory ball mills, colloid mills, centrifugal mills, tumbling ball mills, planetary ball mills, jet mills produces fine particles which increase surface area, reduce cellulose crystallinity, resulting in an improved conversion of sugars polymers during enzymatic hydrolysis. For example, studies have shown that particles sizes must be reduced to 0.5–2 mm in order to reach a well-accepted level of digestibility [22]. Currently, milling processes are not cost-effective because of high investment costs but also high-energy requirements. Total energy requirement (ETER) of milling processes will depend on the physicochemical proprieties of biomass and also on the ratio of particle size distribution of materials before and after milling, which also depend strongly on the equipment or machine used. ETER, glucose yields and energy efficiency are generally used to compare performance and efficiency of different pretreatment processes [10], [14], [15], [21]. However, literature concerning the comparison of energy consumption, and energy efficiency of lignocellulosic biomass remain scarce. This work is a first attempt to compare different milling processes (i.e. BM, VBM, CM, JM) in term of sugars yields after enzymatic hydrolysis, energy requirement and energy efficiency. The physicochemical properties changes, enzymatic digestibility, energy consumption and energy efficiency were evaluated and compared to chemical and physicochemical pretreatment developed in literature for BG biomass. In this study, we investigated the effect of vibro-ball milling (VBM) for 5 and 30 min at a frequency of 20 s−1 on the physicochemical composition and enzymatic hydrolysis (30 U g−1 total solids (TS) of cellulase and endo-1,4-xylanase from Trichoderma longibrachiatum) of dry and wet solid separated digestates from an agricultural biogas plant. We found that VBM of dry solid digestate improved the physical parameters as both the particle size and the crystallinity index (from 27% to 75%) were reduced. By contrast, VBM of wet solid digestate had a minimal effect on the physicochemical parameters. The best results in terms of cellulose and hemicelluloses hydrolysis were noted for 30 min of VBM of dry solid digestate, with hydrolysis yields of 64% and 85% for hemicelluloses and cellulose, respectively. At the condition of 30 min of VBM, bioethanol and methane production on the dry solid separated digestate was investigated. Bioethanol fermentation by simultaneous saccharification and fermentation resulted in an ethanol yield of 98 geth kg−1 TS (corresponding to 90% of the theoretical value) versus 19 geth kg−1 TS for raw solid digestate. Finally, in terms of methane potential, VBM for 30 min lead to an increase of the methane potential of 31% compared to untreated solid digestate. Graphical Abstract 1. Introduction Agricultural wastes represent a vast biomass resource that can readily be converted into sustainable biofuels, chemicals, and other economic by-products by use of a biorefinery concept. As anaerobic digestion has become an efficient technology for waste treatment and renewable energy production, it has resulted in a substantial increase in the use of agricultural anaerobic digesters throughout the EU [1,2]. Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a well-established biological process that has been in use for a long time to anaerobically degrade organic materials into biogas, which is a mixture of CH4 (50–70%) and CO2 (30–50%), and digestate [3]. After a cleaning process, biogas can be further converted into heat and electricity through cogeneration heat and power (CHP) systems [4]. In parallel, biogas can also be upgraded into biomethane through several technologies (e.g., chemical absorption, membrane separation, water scrubbing, pressure swing adsorption, etc.) as a substitute of natural gas or its use as a transport fuel [3]. Digestate is mainly comprised of water (over 90%), residual undegraded fibers (e.g., cellulose, hemicelluloses, and lignin), and inorganic compounds (e.g., ash), and it is generally mechanically separated into liquid and solid fractions that are stored and handled separately [5,6]. Nevertheless, due to the low hydraulic retention times (HRTs) that are generally applied in industrial biogas plants, after which biogas production starts to decrease, part of the organic matter remains in the solid phase of the digestate [7,8]. Consequently, research on alternative valorization routes for solid separated digestate to reduce the environmental impact of disposal and to improve the economic profitability of AD plants is gaining a great interest from the scientific community [5,6]. To date, the valorization strategies that have been investigated are thermochemical processes such as torrefaction and hydrothermal carbonization [9], pyrolysis [4,10], and gasification [11]. Few studies to date have investigated how to use the remaining organic matter present into the solid digestate for sugar platform production and to generate further biofuels such as bioethanol or methane [12,13]. As reported by Santi et al., (2015), digestate produced by commercial agricultural biogas plants still contains a considerable quantity of cell wall polymers [8]. These could potentially be back to AD after a pretreatment step [7] or used in biorefinery processes, for sugar platform production (from C5 and C6) by enzymatic hydrolysis and further generation of biofuels such as bioethanol [14,15]. Nonetheless, due to the recalcitrant properties of the organic matter remaining in solid digestate, a pretreatment step is necessary to improve its biodegradability and further enzymatic hydrolysis and/or biofuel production such as bioethanol or methane by recirculation into the AD process [16,17,18]. Several pretreatment technologies have been tested with agricultural wastes such as physical, thermal, thermochemical, and biological pretreatment, on their own or in combination with each other [17]. Thermal and thermochemical pretreatments have been extensively investigated in terms of their ability to enhance enzymatic hydrolysis and further bioethanol production, although they can also result in potential inhibitors (e.g., furans and polyphenols) generation for microorganisms and strains [19,20]. Another promising option is the use of mechanical pretreatment, which avoids the production of potential inhibitors in addition to improving the physical properties (e.g., the crystallinity, accessible surface area, and particle size) for further enzymatic hydrolysis and/or biofuel production [21,22]. Mini-report on the mechanisms of each milling process

Wet disc milling applies force and creates fiber fragmentation through a combination of shear and compression, with a strong emphasis on controlled wetting to facilitate disintegration. The evidence points to wet milling as a common method for producing cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) by “facilitating efficient disintegration of cellulose” [N1-R1], and to wet disk milling specifically as a method used to investigate dimension changes in microfibrillated cellulose [N1-R5]. The search evidence also links wet milling to mechanical pretreatment of cellulose pulp, where the process is described as a way to improve the mechanical properties and enzymatic digestibility of lignocellulosics [N1-R4]. This suggests that wet disc milling operates by subjecting fibers to repeated shearing and compression forces in a liquid medium, which can reduce fiber size and promote fibrillation rather than extreme fragmentation.

Hammer milling, by contrast, uses impact and shear to break fibers, with a more pronounced role for high-speed impact. The evidence for hammer milling notes that major drawbacks of rotary bypass shear mills include high cost and low throughput compared to hammer mills [N2-R2], and that hammer mill wear is dominated by erosion caused by high-speed impact with biomass [N2-R3]. Another search result explicitly describes milling pretreatment as reducing particle size through compression, shear, and tearing mechanisms [N2-R4]. Taken together, this indicates that hammer milling relies heavily on kinetic energy delivered by rapidly moving hammer blades, which generate both direct impact forces and secondary shear forces as biomass particles collide with each other and the equipment. The result is more direct fragmentation and less controlled fibrillation compared to wet disc milling.

The differences in energy input and fiber interaction are substantial. Wet disc milling appears to be more energy-efficient and selective for controlled fiber disintegration, because the liquid medium and disc geometry allow continuous shear and compression without the extreme shock loads of hammering. The evidence suggests that wet disc milling is often used to produce nanofibrils, which implies a balance between fiber damage and the preservation of some fiber integrity [N1-R1][N1-R5]. Hammer milling, on the other hand, is associated with higher energy input and more aggressive fiber interaction, as the evidence emphasizes high-speed impact, erosion, and tearing mechanisms [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. This means hammer milling can generate more uniform particle size distributions and greater fragmentation, but it also increases the risk of excessive damage and fiber breakage.

In short, wet disc milling relies on controlled shear and compression in a wet environment to produce fibrillation and smaller fibers, while hammer milling uses high-speed impact and shear to break fibers more aggressively. The two processes differ most clearly in how they apply force: wet disc milling is more continuous and selective, whereas hammer milling is more abrupt and energetic [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4].
node_outputs.N8:
Mini-report on structural changes caused by each milling process

The structural changes caused by milling are evident in fiber length, width, surface morphology, damage modes, and wall integrity, with crystallinity also being affected by milling-induced decrystallization and size changes. The evidence repeatedly ties milling to changes in fiber size and crystallinity, showing that mechanical pretreatment can reduce particle size and alter crystallinity [N3-R4][N3-R5]. One source explicitly states that ball-milling pretreatment reduced particle size, crystallinity index (CrI), and degree of polymerization (DP) of MCC significantly, and produced crystallinity and DP reductions [N3-R5]. Another source reports that the evolution of cellulose crystallinity of flax fibers during ball milling was studied, along with mean fiber lengths and diameters [N3-R4]. This indicates that milling changes are not isolated to one property but are part of a broader structural transformation.

Changes in fiber length, width, and surface morphology are directly supported by the evidence. The search result on ball milling notes that the study looked at “mean fibre lengths and diameters” [N3-R4], while the wet disc milling evidence links the process to microfibrillated cellulose and dimension changes [N1-R5]. The fiber morphology evidence further supports that the microstructure and surface texture can be altered: AFM imaging can reveal microfibril structure, surface topography, and other surface features relevant to cellulose fibers [N4-R3][N4-R5]. The evidence also points to the importance of microscopy-based characterization for understanding these changes, including SEM, XRD, and AFM methods [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This means that fiber length reduction, width narrowing, and surface roughening or fibrillation can be measured and interpreted through these techniques.

Damage modes such as fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage are well supported in the evidence. The wet disc milling literature emphasizes the production of CNFs and nanofibrils, which is essentially a fibrillation process [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The fiber damage literature notes that fiber failure mechanisms include tensile, compressive, or shear fracture, local delamination, and fiber breakage [N6-R3], while another source lists failure modes such as fiber splitting, interface decohesion, fiber kinking, and matrix shear failure [N6-R4]. The milling evidence also describes compression, shear, and tearing mechanisms as ways biomass is reduced in size [N2-R4]. Together, these sources indicate that milling can produce fibrillation at the finest scale, delamination through wall separation, and fiber breakage through direct mechanical failure. Hammer milling is especially associated with aggressive damage because of its high-speed impact and erosion-dominated wear [N2-R3][N2-R4], which suggests it is more likely to cause fiber breakage and delamination than wet disc milling.

Effects on fiber wall integrity and crystallinity are closely linked. The dissolution study shows that crystallinity and fiber diameter strongly affect swelling and dissolution behavior, and that fibers of smaller diameter swell more and become amorphous faster [N3-F3]. Another source reports that milling reduced crystallinity index and degree of polymerization, and produced crystallinity and DP reductions [N3-R5]. The crystallinity evidence also notes that when decrystallization is important, thinner fibers increase in solubility more with a reduction in crystallinity than diameter, while when dissolution is controlled by chain disentanglement, or in larger-diameter fibers, milling can increase solubility [N3-F3]. This means milling affects fiber walls by promoting decrystallization and reducing crystallinity, which in turn changes how fibers respond to swelling, dissolution, and mechanical load. The evidence is therefore consistent with the idea that milling-induced damage weakens fiber walls and modifies their crystalline structure [N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3].

Overall, both milling processes cause structural changes, but wet disc milling tends to favor controlled fibrillation and size reduction with some preservation of fiber integrity, while hammer milling tends to produce more aggressive fragmentation and damage. The key structural outcomes are shorter fibers, narrower diameters, altered surface morphology, fibrillation or delamination, fiber breakage, and reduced crystallinity [N1-R1][N1-R5][N2-R4][N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3].
node_outputs.N9:
Mini-report on how the processes compare in practical fiber outcomes

Wet disc milling and hammer milling differ substantially in their practical fiber outcomes, especially in terms of uniformity, damage, energy use, and suitability for downstream applications. The evidence and upstream reports together suggest that wet disc milling is generally more favorable when the goal is controlled fiber fragmentation and fibrillation, while hammer milling is more aggressive and better suited for rapid size reduction at the expense of increased damage [N1-R1][N1-R5][N2-R2][N2-R4].

On uniformity and damage, wet disc milling tends to produce more uniform or at least more controlled fiber outcomes. The evidence points to wet disc milling as a method used to produce microfibrillated cellulose and to investigate dimension changes in microfibrillated cellulose, which implies a deliberate process aimed at controlled fibrillation rather than random fragmentation [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The upstream mechanism report also describes wet disc milling as applying force through shear and compression in a wet environment, which is more selective than the high-speed impact of hammer milling [N1-R1][N1-R4]. In contrast, hammer milling is associated with more aggressive damage because of high-speed impact, erosion, and tearing mechanisms, which increases the likelihood of fiber breakage and delamination [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The damage modes literature further supports that milling can produce fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage, with hammer-like processes being especially prone to fiber breakage [N6-R3][N6-R4]. So, wet disc milling is more likely to produce fibers with a more uniform fibrillation profile, while hammer milling is more likely to produce more damaged fibers with more breakage and delamination [N1-R1][N2-R2][N6-R3].

The trade-offs between fiber yield, damage, and processing energy are clear. The comparison evidence notes that fine and/or ultrafine milling processes such as ball milling, vibratory ball milling, and centrifugal milling are simpler saccharification technologies that do not require chemical or water inputs and minimize waste generation [N5-F1]. This suggests that wet disc milling and hammer milling both fall within the broader category of mechanical fractionation, but their energy profiles differ. The upstream mechanism report indicates that hammer milling is associated with higher energy input and more aggressive fiber interaction, while wet disc milling appears more energy-efficient and selective for controlled disintegration [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The structural evidence also shows that milling can reduce crystallinity, particle size, and fiber dimensions, but that the degree of damage depends on the process: wet disc milling promotes fibrillation, while hammer milling promotes fragmentation and can increase damage [N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3]. The comparison evidence further reports that VBM was the most effective in decreasing cellulose crystallinity, BM was the most effective in increasing surface area, and CM was the most energy-efficient in terms of energy-efficiency (kg glucose/kWh) [N5-R1][N5-F1]. Taken together, the practical trade-off is that hammer milling can achieve higher surface area and finer particles, but at greater damage and energy cost, whereas wet disc milling can preserve some fiber integrity and produce more controlled fibrillation at lower damage and more moderate energy use [N2-R4][N5-R1][N5-F1].

For downstream applications, the choice between wet disc milling and hammer milling depends on the target properties. The comparison evidence explicitly states that mechanical fractionation of lignocellulosic biomass can improve enzymatic hydrolysis by reducing particle size and cellulose crystallinity, which increases accessible surface area and improves sugar conversion [N5-F1]. Wet disc milling is therefore attractive when downstream processing requires well-dispersed fibrillated fibers, such as in nanocellulose production, composite reinforcement, or high-surface-area functional materials [N1-R1][N1-R5]. Hammer milling, by contrast, is preferred when rapid size reduction and high particle yield are needed, especially if downstream processing is more tolerant of some damage or if the goal is to maximize surface area for enzymatic hydrolysis or biofuel conversion [N5-F1][N5-R1]. The upstream structural report also notes that milling-induced damage can weaken fiber walls and modify crystallinity, which matters for applications such as dissolution, swelling, and composite performance [N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3]. So, wet disc milling is usually preferred when fiber integrity and controlled fibrillation matter, while hammer milling is preferred when rapid fragmentation and high yield matter [N1-R1][N2-R4][N5-F1].

Overall, the practical difference is that wet disc milling produces more uniform or more controlled fibers with less damage, while hammer milling produces more damaged fibers with higher fragmentation and greater energy input. The best downstream match depends on whether the process needs controlled fibrillation, high surface area, or rapid size reduction [N1-R1][N2-R4][N5-F1].
node_outputs.N10:
Integrated final answer on differences between wet disc and hammer milling

## 1) Core difference: mechanism and how force is applied

Wet disc milling and hammer milling differ fundamentally in how they apply force to lignocellulosic fibers. Wet disc milling uses controlled shear and compression in a wet environment to create fiber fragmentation, fibrillation, and smaller fiber dimensions. The evidence describes it as a method that facilitates efficient disintegration of cellulose and is used to produce microfibrillated cellulose [N1-R1][N1-R5]. It also appears as a mechanical pretreatment that improves the mechanical properties and enzymatic digestibility of lignocellulosics [N1-R4]. This means wet disc milling is more continuous and selective, relying on repeated shearing and compression rather than sudden impact.

Hammer milling, by contrast, relies heavily on high-speed impact and secondary shear forces to break fibers. The evidence notes that hammer mills are associated with high-speed impact and erosion-dominated wear, with major drawbacks including high cost and low throughput compared to hammer mills [N2-R2][N2-R3]. It also describes milling pretreatment as reducing particle size through compression, shear, and tearing mechanisms [N2-R4]. This makes hammer milling more aggressive: it delivers abrupt kinetic energy to the biomass, which can generate more direct fragmentation and more severe fiber damage than wet disc milling.

The difference in energy input and fiber interaction is therefore clear. Wet disc milling appears more energy-efficient and less damaging because it uses controlled wetting and continuous shear/compression forces [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Hammer milling, however, is associated with higher energy input and more aggressive fiber interaction, because of its reliance on high-speed impact and erosion [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. In short, wet disc milling is more like a controlled grinding process, while hammer milling is more like a high-energy impact process.

## 2) Structural changes: fiber length, width, and surface morphology

Both processes change the structure of lignocellulosic fibers, but the nature of the changes differs. The structural evidence shows that milling alters fiber length, width, and surface morphology, and that these effects are measurable through microscopy and other characterization methods [N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3][N4-R3][N4-R5]. The evidence also supports the use of SEM, XRD, and AFM for studying cellulose fiber structure [N4-R1][N4-R2].

Wet disc milling tends to produce more controlled reductions in fiber size. The wet disc milling evidence points to microfibrillated cellulose and dimension changes, which suggests that the process favors fibrillation and controlled shortening rather than random fragmentation [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The structural evidence also notes that milling can reduce crystallinity and particle size, and that fibers of smaller diameter swell more and become amorphous faster [N3-F3]. This implies that wet disc milling can produce fibers with a narrower size distribution and more uniform fibrillation, while preserving some structural integrity.

Hammer milling, by contrast, tends to produce more aggressive fragmentation. The evidence describes compression, shear, and tearing mechanisms as ways biomass is reduced in size [N2-R4]. It also associates hammer milling with higher damage and fiber breakage because of high-speed impact and erosion [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The damage modes evidence further supports that milling can produce fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage, with fiber failure mechanisms including tensile, compressive, or shear fracture, local delamination, and fiber breakage [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This means hammer milling can create shorter fibers, but often with more irregular morphology and more breakage.

## 3) Damage modes: fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage

The two processes differ in the dominant damage modes they induce. Wet disc milling is associated with fibrillation, which is the fine-scale unraveling of fiber walls into nanofibrils. The evidence explicitly links wet disc milling to microfibrillated cellulose production and to dimension changes in microfibrillated cellulose [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The structural evidence also shows that milling can weaken fiber walls and modify crystallinity, which supports the idea that wet disc milling induces controlled fibrillation rather than severe breakage [N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3].

Hammer milling, by contrast, is more associated with delamination and fiber breakage. The damage modes evidence notes that fiber failure mechanisms include local delamination and fiber breakage [N6-R3]. The evidence also mentions that milling pretreatment can produce fiber splitting, interface decohesion, fiber kinking, and matrix shear failure [N6-R4]. The upstream mechanism report adds that hammer milling is associated with high-speed impact, erosion, and tearing mechanisms, which are consistent with more severe wall damage and breakage [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. So, wet disc milling is more likely to produce a fibrillated, well-dispersed structure, while hammer milling is more likely to produce shorter fibers with more delamination and breakage.

## 4) Effects on fiber wall integrity and crystallinity

Both processes affect fiber wall integrity and crystallinity, but in different ways. The structural evidence shows that milling can reduce crystallinity index and degree of polymerization, and that it can produce crystallinity and DP reductions [N3-R5]. The dissolution study further notes that crystallinity and fiber diameter strongly affect swelling and dissolution behavior, and that fibers of smaller diameter swell more and become amorphous faster [N3-F3]. This means that milling-induced damage weakens fiber walls and can promote decrystallization.

Wet disc milling appears to preserve more wall integrity relative to hammer milling because it uses controlled shear and compression in a wet environment. The evidence suggests that wet disc milling is used to produce nanofibrils and to investigate microfibrillated cellulose, which implies that it can reduce crystallinity while still maintaining some fibrillation and fiber structure [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The comparison evidence also supports that mechanical fractionation can reduce particle size and cellulose crystallinity, which improves enzymatic hydrolysis [N5-F1].

Hammer milling, by contrast, is more likely to damage fiber walls because of its aggressive impact and tearing mechanisms [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The evidence also shows that milling can increase surface area, reduce crystallinity index, and lower crystallinity, but that the process is more damaging overall [N5-R1][N5-F1]. So, the wall-integrity trade-off is that wet disc milling tends to weaken walls less and produce a more controlled fibrillated structure, while hammer milling tends to weaken walls more and produce more fragmented fibers.

## 5) Practical fiber outcomes: uniformity, damage, and energy trade-offs

The practical difference between wet disc milling and hammer milling is most evident in the balance between uniformity, damage, and energy use. Wet disc milling tends to produce more uniform or more controlled fibers. The evidence and branch report both point to wet disc milling as a method used for microfibrillated cellulose and as a process that can produce dimension changes in a controlled way [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The mechanism report also describes it as applying force through shear and compression in a wet environment, which is more selective than the high-speed impact of hammer milling [N1-R1][N1-R4]. This makes wet disc milling especially attractive when the goal is controlled fiber fragmentation and fibrillation.

Hammer milling, by contrast, tends to produce more damaged fibers. The evidence notes that hammer milling is associated with high-speed impact, erosion, and tearing mechanisms, which increases the likelihood of fiber breakage and delamination [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The damage modes evidence also supports that milling can produce fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage, with hammer-like processes being especially prone to breakage [N6-R3][N6-R4]. So, hammer milling can achieve a finer particle size distribution, but at the cost of more damage and less uniformity.

The energy trade-off is also important. The comparison evidence notes that fine and/or ultrafine milling processes such as ball milling, vibratory ball milling, and centrifugal milling are simpler saccharification technologies that do not require chemical or water inputs and minimize waste generation [N5-F1]. This suggests that both wet disc milling and hammer milling fall within the broader category of mechanical fractionation, but their energy profiles differ. The mechanism report indicates that hammer milling is associated with higher energy input and more aggressive fiber interaction, while wet disc milling appears more energy-efficient and selective [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The comparison evidence also reports that VBM was the most effective in decreasing cellulose crystallinity, BM was the most effective in increasing surface area, and CM was the most energy-efficient in terms of energy-efficiency (kg glucose/kWh) [N5-R1][N5-F1]. Taken together, the practical trade-off is that hammer milling can achieve higher surface area and finer particles, but at greater damage and energy cost, whereas wet disc milling can preserve some fiber integrity and produce more controlled fibrillation at lower damage and more moderate energy use [N2-R4][N5-R1][N5-F1].

## 6) Context for downstream applications

The choice between wet disc milling and hammer milling depends on the downstream application. Wet disc milling is usually preferred when the goal is well-dispersed fibrillated fibers, such as in nanocellulose production, composite reinforcement, or high-surface-area functional materials [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The evidence also suggests that wet disc milling can improve enzymatic hydrolysis by producing fibers and reducing crystallinity [N1-R4][N5-F1]. This makes it suitable for applications where fiber integrity and controlled fibrillation matter more than maximum fragmentation.

Hammer milling is usually preferred when rapid size reduction and high particle yield are needed, especially if downstream processing is more tolerant of some damage or if the goal is to maximize surface area for enzymatic hydrolysis or biofuel conversion [N5-F1][N5-R1]. The evidence also notes that mechanical fractionation can improve enzymatic hydrolysis by reducing particle size and cellulose crystallinity [N5-F1]. So, hammer milling is attractive for industrial applications where speed and yield matter more than uniformity.

## 7) Bottom line

Overall, wet disc milling and hammer milling differ in several key ways:

- **Mechanism**: wet disc milling uses controlled shear and compression in a wet environment; hammer milling uses high-speed impact and shear [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4].
- **Structural effects**: wet disc milling tends to produce more controlled fibrillation and smaller fibers, while hammer milling tends to produce more fragmented fibers with more delamination and breakage [N1-R1][N1-R5][N2-R2][N2-R4][N6-R3][N6-R4].
- **Damage modes**: wet disc milling favors fibrillation, while hammer milling favors delamination and fiber breakage [N6-R3][N6-R4].
- **Crystallinity and wall integrity**: both reduce crystallinity, but wet disc milling generally preserves more wall integrity than hammer milling [N3-R5][N3-F3].
- **Practical outcomes**: wet disc milling is more uniform and less damaging, while hammer milling is more aggressive and more energy-intensive [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N5-F1].
- **Downstream context**: wet disc milling is better for controlled fibrillation and nanocellulose, while hammer milling is better for rapid fragmentation and high-yield processing [N1-R1][N1-R5][N5-F1].

In short, wet disc milling is the controlled, selective process for fibrillated fibers, whereas hammer milling is the more aggressive process for rapid fragmentation and size reduction.

Mini-report on the mechanisms of each milling process

Wet disc milling applies force and creates fiber fragmentation through a combination of shear and compression, with a strong emphasis on controlled wetting to facilitate disintegration. The evidence points to wet milling as a common method for producing cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) by “facilitating efficient disintegration of cellulose” [N1-R1], and to wet disk milling specifically as a method used to investigate dimension changes in microfibrillated cellulose [N1-R5]. The search evidence also links wet milling to mechanical pretreatment of cellulose pulp, where the process is described as a way to improve the mechanical properties and enzymatic digestibility of lignocellulosics [N1-R4]. This suggests that wet disc milling operates by subjecting fibers to repeated shearing and compression forces in a liquid medium, which can reduce fiber size and promote fibrillation rather than extreme fragmentation.

Hammer milling, by contrast, uses impact and shear to break fibers, with a more pronounced role for high-speed impact. The evidence for hammer milling notes that major drawbacks of rotary bypass shear mills include high cost and low throughput compared to hammer mills [N2-R2], and that hammer mill wear is dominated by erosion caused by high-speed impact with biomass [N2-R3]. Another search result explicitly describes milling pretreatment as reducing particle size through compression, shear, and tearing mechanisms [N2-R4]. Taken together, this indicates that hammer milling relies heavily on kinetic energy delivered by rapidly moving hammer blades, which generate both direct impact forces and secondary shear forces as biomass particles collide with each other and the equipment. The result is more direct fragmentation and less controlled fibrillation compared to wet disc milling.

The differences in energy input and fiber interaction are substantial. Wet disc milling appears to be more energy-efficient and selective for controlled fiber disintegration, because the liquid medium and disc geometry allow continuous shear and compression without the extreme shock loads of hammering. The evidence suggests that wet disc milling is often used to produce nanofibrils, which implies a balance between fiber damage and the preservation of some fiber integrity [N1-R1][N1-R5]. Hammer milling, on the other hand, is associated with higher energy input and more aggressive fiber interaction, as the evidence emphasizes high-speed impact, erosion, and tearing mechanisms [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. This means hammer milling can generate more uniform particle size distributions and greater fragmentation, but it also increases the risk of excessive damage and fiber breakage.

In short, wet disc milling relies on controlled shear and compression in a wet environment to produce fibrillation and smaller fibers, while hammer milling uses high-speed impact and shear to break fibers more aggressively. The two processes differ most clearly in how they apply force: wet disc milling is more continuous and selective, whereas hammer milling is more abrupt and energetic [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4].

Mini-report on structural changes caused by each milling process

The structural changes caused by milling are evident in fiber length, width, surface morphology, damage modes, and wall integrity, with crystallinity also being affected by milling-induced decrystallization and size changes. The evidence repeatedly ties milling to changes in fiber size and crystallinity, showing that mechanical pretreatment can reduce particle size and alter crystallinity [N3-R4][N3-R5]. One source explicitly states that ball-milling pretreatment reduced particle size, crystallinity index (CrI), and degree of polymerization (DP) of MCC significantly, and produced crystallinity and DP reductions [N3-R5]. Another source reports that the evolution of cellulose crystallinity of flax fibers during ball milling was studied, along with mean fiber lengths and diameters [N3-R4]. This indicates that milling changes are not isolated to one property but are part of a broader structural transformation.

Changes in fiber length, width, and surface morphology are directly supported by the evidence. The search result on ball milling notes that the study looked at “mean fibre lengths and diameters” [N3-R4], while the wet disc milling evidence links the process to microfibrillated cellulose and dimension changes [N1-R5]. The fiber morphology evidence further supports that the microstructure and surface texture can be altered: AFM imaging can reveal microfibril structure, surface topography, and other surface features relevant to cellulose fibers [N4-R3][N4-R5]. The evidence also points to the importance of microscopy-based characterization for understanding these changes, including SEM, XRD, and AFM methods [N4-R1][N4-R2]. This means that fiber length reduction, width narrowing, and surface roughening or fibrillation can be measured and interpreted through these techniques.

Damage modes such as fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage are well supported in the evidence. The wet disc milling literature emphasizes the production of CNFs and nanofibrils, which is essentially a fibrillation process [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The fiber damage literature notes that fiber failure mechanisms include tensile, compressive, or shear fracture, local delamination, and fiber breakage [N6-R3], while another source lists failure modes such as fiber splitting, interface decohesion, fiber kinking, and matrix shear failure [N6-R4]. The milling evidence also describes compression, shear, and tearing mechanisms as ways biomass is reduced in size [N2-R4]. Together, these sources indicate that milling can produce fibrillation at the finest scale, delamination through wall separation, and fiber breakage through direct mechanical failure. Hammer milling is especially associated with aggressive damage because of its high-speed impact and erosion-dominated wear [N2-R3][N2-R4], which suggests it is more likely to cause fiber breakage and delamination than wet disc milling.

Effects on fiber wall integrity and crystallinity are closely linked. The dissolution study shows that crystallinity and fiber diameter strongly affect swelling and dissolution behavior, and that fibers of smaller diameter swell more and become amorphous faster [N3-F3]. Another source reports that milling reduced crystallinity index and degree of polymerization, and produced crystallinity and DP reductions [N3-R5]. The crystallinity evidence also notes that when decrystallization is important, thinner fibers increase in solubility more with a reduction in crystallinity than diameter, while when dissolution is controlled by chain disentanglement, or in larger-diameter fibers, milling can increase solubility [N3-F3]. This means milling affects fiber walls by promoting decrystallization and reducing crystallinity, which in turn changes how fibers respond to swelling, dissolution, and mechanical load. The evidence is therefore consistent with the idea that milling-induced damage weakens fiber walls and modifies their crystalline structure [N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3].

Overall, both milling processes cause structural changes, but wet disc milling tends to favor controlled fibrillation and size reduction with some preservation of fiber integrity, while hammer milling tends to produce more aggressive fragmentation and damage. The key structural outcomes are shorter fibers, narrower diameters, altered surface morphology, fibrillation or delamination, fiber breakage, and reduced crystallinity [N1-R1][N1-R5][N2-R4][N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3].

Integrated final answer on differences between wet disc and hammer milling

## 1) Core difference: mechanism and how force is applied

Wet disc milling and hammer milling differ fundamentally in how they apply force to lignocellulosic fibers. Wet disc milling uses controlled shear and compression in a wet environment to create fiber fragmentation, fibrillation, and smaller fiber dimensions. The evidence describes it as a method that facilitates efficient disintegration of cellulose and is used to produce microfibrillated cellulose [N1-R1][N1-R5]. It also appears as a mechanical pretreatment that improves the mechanical properties and enzymatic digestibility of lignocellulosics [N1-R4]. This means wet disc milling is more continuous and selective, relying on repeated shearing and compression rather than sudden impact.

Hammer milling, by contrast, relies heavily on high-speed impact and secondary shear forces to break fibers. The evidence notes that hammer mills are associated with high-speed impact and erosion-dominated wear, with major drawbacks including high cost and low throughput compared to hammer mills [N2-R2][N2-R3]. It also describes milling pretreatment as reducing particle size through compression, shear, and tearing mechanisms [N2-R4]. This makes hammer milling more aggressive: it delivers abrupt kinetic energy to the biomass, which can generate more direct fragmentation and more severe fiber damage than wet disc milling.

The difference in energy input and fiber interaction is therefore clear. Wet disc milling appears more energy-efficient and less damaging because it uses controlled wetting and continuous shear/compression forces [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Hammer milling, however, is associated with higher energy input and more aggressive fiber interaction, because of its reliance on high-speed impact and erosion [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. In short, wet disc milling is more like a controlled grinding process, while hammer milling is more like a high-energy impact process.

## 2) Structural changes: fiber length, width, and surface morphology

Both processes change the structure of lignocellulosic fibers, but the nature of the changes differs. The structural evidence shows that milling alters fiber length, width, and surface morphology, and that these effects are measurable through microscopy and other characterization methods [N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3][N4-R3][N4-R5]. The evidence also supports the use of SEM, XRD, and AFM for studying cellulose fiber structure [N4-R1][N4-R2].

Wet disc milling tends to produce more controlled reductions in fiber size. The wet disc milling evidence points to microfibrillated cellulose and dimension changes, which suggests that the process favors fibrillation and controlled shortening rather than random fragmentation [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The structural evidence also notes that milling can reduce crystallinity and particle size, and that fibers of smaller diameter swell more and become amorphous faster [N3-F3]. This implies that wet disc milling can produce fibers with a narrower size distribution and more uniform fibrillation, while preserving some structural integrity.

Hammer milling, by contrast, tends to produce more aggressive fragmentation. The evidence describes compression, shear, and tearing mechanisms as ways biomass is reduced in size [N2-R4]. It also associates hammer milling with higher damage and fiber breakage because of high-speed impact and erosion [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The damage modes evidence further supports that milling can produce fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage, with fiber failure mechanisms including tensile, compressive, or shear fracture, local delamination, and fiber breakage [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This means hammer milling can create shorter fibers, but often with more irregular morphology and more breakage.

## 3) Damage modes: fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage

The two processes differ in the dominant damage modes they induce. Wet disc milling is associated with fibrillation, which is the fine-scale unraveling of fiber walls into nanofibrils. The evidence explicitly links wet disc milling to microfibrillated cellulose production and to dimension changes in microfibrillated cellulose [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The structural evidence also shows that milling can weaken fiber walls and modify crystallinity, which supports the idea that wet disc milling induces controlled fibrillation rather than severe breakage [N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3].

Hammer milling, by contrast, is more associated with delamination and fiber breakage. The damage modes evidence notes that fiber failure mechanisms include local delamination and fiber breakage [N6-R3]. The evidence also mentions that milling pretreatment can produce fiber splitting, interface decohesion, fiber kinking, and matrix shear failure [N6-R4]. The upstream mechanism report adds that hammer milling is associated with high-speed impact, erosion, and tearing mechanisms, which are consistent with more severe wall damage and breakage [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. So, wet disc milling is more likely to produce a fibrillated, well-dispersed structure, while hammer milling is more likely to produce shorter fibers with more delamination and breakage.

## 4) Effects on fiber wall integrity and crystallinity

Both processes affect fiber wall integrity and crystallinity, but in different ways. The structural evidence shows that milling can reduce crystallinity index and degree of polymerization, and that it can produce crystallinity and DP reductions [N3-R5]. The dissolution study further notes that crystallinity and fiber diameter strongly affect swelling and dissolution behavior, and that fibers of smaller diameter swell more and become amorphous faster [N3-F3]. This means that milling-induced damage weakens fiber walls and can promote decrystallization.

Wet disc milling appears to preserve more wall integrity relative to hammer milling because it uses controlled shear and compression in a wet environment. The evidence suggests that wet disc milling is used to produce nanofibrils and to investigate microfibrillated cellulose, which implies that it can reduce crystallinity while still maintaining some fibrillation and fiber structure [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The comparison evidence also supports that mechanical fractionation can reduce particle size and cellulose crystallinity, which improves enzymatic hydrolysis [N5-F1].

Hammer milling, by contrast, is more likely to damage fiber walls because of its aggressive impact and tearing mechanisms [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The evidence also shows that milling can increase surface area, reduce crystallinity index, and lower crystallinity, but that the process is more damaging overall [N5-R1][N5-F1]. So, the wall-integrity trade-off is that wet disc milling tends to weaken walls less and produce a more controlled fibrillated structure, while hammer milling tends to weaken walls more and produce more fragmented fibers.

## 5) Practical fiber outcomes: uniformity, damage, and energy trade-offs

The practical difference between wet disc milling and hammer milling is most evident in the balance between uniformity, damage, and energy use. Wet disc milling tends to produce more uniform or more controlled fibers. The evidence and branch report both point to wet disc milling as a method used for microfibrillated cellulose and as a process that can produce dimension changes in a controlled way [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The mechanism report also describes it as applying force through shear and compression in a wet environment, which is more selective than the high-speed impact of hammer milling [N1-R1][N1-R4]. This makes wet disc milling especially attractive when the goal is controlled fiber fragmentation and fibrillation.

Hammer milling, by contrast, tends to produce more damaged fibers. The evidence notes that hammer milling is associated with high-speed impact, erosion, and tearing mechanisms, which increases the likelihood of fiber breakage and delamination [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The damage modes evidence also supports that milling can produce fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage, with hammer-like processes being especially prone to breakage [N6-R3][N6-R4]. So, hammer milling can achieve a finer particle size distribution, but at the cost of more damage and less uniformity.

The energy trade-off is also important. The comparison evidence notes that fine and/or ultrafine milling processes such as ball milling, vibratory ball milling, and centrifugal milling are simpler saccharification technologies that do not require chemical or water inputs and minimize waste generation [N5-F1]. This suggests that both wet disc milling and hammer milling fall within the broader category of mechanical fractionation, but their energy profiles differ. The mechanism report indicates that hammer milling is associated with higher energy input and more aggressive fiber interaction, while wet disc milling appears more energy-efficient and selective [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The comparison evidence also reports that VBM was the most effective in decreasing cellulose crystallinity, BM was the most effective in increasing surface area, and CM was the most energy-efficient in terms of energy-efficiency (kg glucose/kWh) [N5-R1][N5-F1]. Taken together, the practical trade-off is that hammer milling can achieve higher surface area and finer particles, but at greater damage and energy cost, whereas wet disc milling can preserve some fiber integrity and produce more controlled fibrillation at lower damage and more moderate energy use [N2-R4][N5-R1][N5-F1].

## 6) Context for downstream applications

The choice between wet disc milling and hammer milling depends on the downstream application. Wet disc milling is usually preferred when the goal is well-dispersed fibrillated fibers, such as in nanocellulose production, composite reinforcement, or high-surface-area functional materials [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The evidence also suggests that wet disc milling can improve enzymatic hydrolysis by producing fibers and reducing crystallinity [N1-R4][N5-F1]. This makes it suitable for applications where fiber integrity and controlled fibrillation matter more than maximum fragmentation.

Hammer milling is usually preferred when rapid size reduction and high particle yield are needed, especially if downstream processing is more tolerant of some damage or if the goal is to maximize surface area for enzymatic hydrolysis or biofuel conversion [N5-F1][N5-R1]. The evidence also notes that mechanical fractionation can improve enzymatic hydrolysis by reducing particle size and cellulose crystallinity [N5-F1]. So, hammer milling is attractive for industrial applications where speed and yield matter more than uniformity.

## 7) Bottom line

Overall, wet disc milling and hammer milling differ in several key ways:

- **Mechanism**: wet disc milling uses controlled shear and compression in a wet environment; hammer milling uses high-speed impact and shear [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4].
- **Structural effects**: wet disc milling tends to produce more controlled fibrillation and smaller fibers, while hammer milling tends to produce more fragmented fibers with more delamination and breakage [N1-R1][N1-R5][N2-R2][N2-R4][N6-R3][N6-R4].
- **Damage modes**: wet disc milling favors fibrillation, while hammer milling favors delamination and fiber breakage [N6-R3][N6-R4].
- **Crystallinity and wall integrity**: both reduce crystallinity, but wet disc milling generally preserves more wall integrity than hammer milling [N3-R5][N3-F3].
- **Practical outcomes**: wet disc milling is more uniform and less damaging, while hammer milling is more aggressive and more energy-intensive [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N5-F1].
- **Downstream context**: wet disc milling is better for controlled fibrillation and nanocellulose, while hammer milling is better for rapid fragmentation and high-yield processing [N1-R1][N1-R5][N5-F1].

In short, wet disc milling is the controlled, selective process for fibrillated fibers, whereas hammer milling is the more aggressive process for rapid fragmentation and size reduction.

Wet disc milling applies force and creates fiber fragmentation through a combination of shear and compression, with a strong emphasis on controlled wetting to facilitate disintegration. The evidence points to wet milling as a common method for producing cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) by “facilitating efficient disintegration of cellulose” [N1-R1], and to wet disk milling specifically as a method used to investigate dimension changes in microfibrillated cellulose [N1-R5]. The search evidence also links wet milling to mechanical pretreatment of cellulose pulp, where the process is described as a way to improve the mechanical properties and enzymatic digestibility of lignocellulosics [N1-R4]. This suggests that wet disc milling operates by subjecting fibers to repeated shearing and compression forces in a liquid medium, which can reduce fiber size and promote fibrillation rather than extreme fragmentation.

Hammer milling, by contrast, uses impact and shear to break fibers, with a more pronounced role for high-speed impact. The evidence for hammer milling notes that major drawbacks of rotary bypass shear mills include high cost and low throughput compared to hammer mills [N2-R2], and that hammer mill wear is dominated by erosion caused by high-speed impact with biomass [N2-R3]. Another search result explicitly describes milling pretreatment as reducing particle size through compression, shear, and tearing mechanisms [N2-R4]. Taken together, this indicates that hammer milling relies heavily on kinetic energy delivered by rapidly moving hammer blades, which generate both direct impact forces and secondary shear forces as biomass particles collide with each other and the equipment. The result is more direct fragmentation and less controlled fibrillation compared to wet disc milling.

The differences in energy input and fiber interaction are substantial. Wet disc milling appears to be more energy-efficient and selective for controlled fiber disintegration, because the liquid medium and disc geometry allow continuous shear and compression without the extreme shock loads of hammering. The evidence suggests that wet disc milling is often used to produce nanofibrils, which implies a balance between fiber damage and the preservation of some fiber integrity [N1-R1][N1-R5]. Hammer milling, on the other hand, is associated with higher energy input and more aggressive fiber interaction, as the evidence emphasizes high-speed impact, erosion, and tearing mechanisms [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. This means hammer milling can generate more uniform particle size distributions and greater fragmentation, but it also increases the risk of excessive damage and fiber breakage.

In short, wet disc milling relies on controlled shear and compression in a wet environment to produce fibrillation and smaller fibers, while hammer milling uses high-speed impact and shear to break fibers more aggressively. The two processes differ most clearly in how they apply force: wet disc milling is more continuous and selective, whereas hammer milling is more abrupt and energetic [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4].

Integrated final answer on differences between wet disc and hammer milling

## 1) Core difference: mechanism and how force is applied

Wet disc milling and hammer milling differ fundamentally in how they apply force to lignocellulosic fibers. Wet disc milling uses controlled shear and compression in a wet environment to create fiber fragmentation, fibrillation, and smaller fiber dimensions. The evidence describes it as a method that facilitates efficient disintegration of cellulose and is used to produce microfibrillated cellulose [N1-R1][N1-R5]. It also appears as a mechanical pretreatment that improves the mechanical properties and enzymatic digestibility of lignocellulosics [N1-R4]. This means wet disc milling is more continuous and selective, relying on repeated shearing and compression rather than sudden impact.

Hammer milling, by contrast, relies heavily on high-speed impact and secondary shear forces to break fibers. The evidence notes that hammer mills are associated with high-speed impact and erosion-dominated wear, with major drawbacks including high cost and low throughput compared to hammer mills [N2-R2][N2-R3]. It also describes milling pretreatment as reducing particle size through compression, shear, and tearing mechanisms [N2-R4]. This makes hammer milling more aggressive: it delivers abrupt kinetic energy to the biomass, which can generate more direct fragmentation and more severe fiber damage than wet disc milling.

The difference in energy input and fiber interaction is therefore clear. Wet disc milling appears more energy-efficient and less damaging because it uses controlled wetting and continuous shear/compression forces [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Hammer milling, however, is associated with higher energy input and more aggressive fiber interaction, because of its reliance on high-speed impact and erosion [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. In short, wet disc milling is more like a controlled grinding process, while hammer milling is more like a high-energy impact process.

## 2) Structural changes: fiber length, width, and surface morphology

Both processes change the structure of lignocellulosic fibers, but the nature of the changes differs. The structural evidence shows that milling alters fiber length, width, and surface morphology, and that these effects are measurable through microscopy and other characterization methods [N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3][N4-R3][N4-R5]. The evidence also supports the use of SEM, XRD, and AFM for studying cellulose fiber structure [N4-R1][N4-R2].

Wet disc milling tends to produce more controlled reductions in fiber size. The wet disc milling evidence points to microfibrillated cellulose and dimension changes, which suggests that the process favors fibrillation and controlled shortening rather than random fragmentation [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The structural evidence also notes that milling can reduce crystallinity and particle size, and that fibers of smaller diameter swell more and become amorphous faster [N3-F3]. This implies that wet disc milling can produce fibers with a narrower size distribution and more uniform fibrillation, while preserving some structural integrity.

Hammer milling, by contrast, tends to produce more aggressive fragmentation. The evidence describes compression, shear, and tearing mechanisms as ways biomass is reduced in size [N2-R4]. It also associates hammer milling with higher damage and fiber breakage because of high-speed impact and erosion [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The damage modes evidence further supports that milling can produce fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage, with fiber failure mechanisms including tensile, compressive, or shear fracture, local delamination, and fiber breakage [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This means hammer milling can create shorter fibers, but often with more irregular morphology and more breakage.

## 3) Damage modes: fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage

The two processes differ in the dominant damage modes they induce. Wet disc milling is associated with fibrillation, which is the fine-scale unraveling of fiber walls into nanofibrils. The evidence explicitly links wet disc milling to microfibrillated cellulose production and to dimension changes in microfibrillated cellulose [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The structural evidence also shows that milling can weaken fiber walls and modify crystallinity, which supports the idea that wet disc milling induces controlled fibrillation rather than severe breakage [N3-R4][N3-R5][N3-F3].

Hammer milling, by contrast, is more associated with delamination and fiber breakage. The damage modes evidence notes that fiber failure mechanisms include local delamination and fiber breakage [N6-R3]. The evidence also mentions that milling pretreatment can produce fiber splitting, interface decohesion, fiber kinking, and matrix shear failure [N6-R4]. The upstream mechanism report adds that hammer milling is associated with high-speed impact, erosion, and tearing mechanisms, which are consistent with more severe wall damage and breakage [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. So, wet disc milling is more likely to produce a fibrillated, well-dispersed structure, while hammer milling is more likely to produce shorter fibers with more delamination and breakage.

## 4) Effects on fiber wall integrity and crystallinity

Both processes affect fiber wall integrity and crystallinity, but in different ways. The structural evidence shows that milling can reduce crystallinity index and degree of polymerization, and that it can produce crystallinity and DP reductions [N3-R5]. The dissolution study further notes that crystallinity and fiber diameter strongly affect swelling and dissolution behavior, and that fibers of smaller diameter swell more and become amorphous faster [N3-F3]. This means that milling-induced damage weakens fiber walls and can promote decrystallization.

Wet disc milling appears to preserve more wall integrity relative to hammer milling because it uses controlled shear and compression in a wet environment. The evidence suggests that wet disc milling is used to produce nanofibrils and to investigate microfibrillated cellulose, which implies that it can reduce crystallinity while still maintaining some fibrillation and fiber structure [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The comparison evidence also supports that mechanical fractionation can reduce particle size and cellulose crystallinity, which improves enzymatic hydrolysis [N5-F1].

Hammer milling, by contrast, is more likely to damage fiber walls because of its aggressive impact and tearing mechanisms [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The evidence also shows that milling can increase surface area, reduce crystallinity index, and lower crystallinity, but that the process is more damaging overall [N5-R1][N5-F1]. So, the wall-integrity trade-off is that wet disc milling tends to weaken walls less and produce a more controlled fibrillated structure, while hammer milling tends to weaken walls more and produce more fragmented fibers.

## 5) Practical fiber outcomes: uniformity, damage, and energy trade-offs

The practical difference between wet disc milling and hammer milling is most evident in the balance between uniformity, damage, and energy use. Wet disc milling tends to produce more uniform or more controlled fibers. The evidence and branch report both point to wet disc milling as a method used for microfibrillated cellulose and as a process that can produce dimension changes in a controlled way [N1-R1][N1-R5]. The mechanism report also describes it as applying force through shear and compression in a wet environment, which is more selective than the high-speed impact of hammer milling [N1-R1][N1-R4]. This makes wet disc milling especially attractive when the goal is controlled fiber fragmentation and fibrillation.

Hammer milling, by contrast, tends to produce more damaged fibers. The evidence notes that hammer milling is associated with high-speed impact, erosion, and tearing mechanisms, which increases the likelihood of fiber breakage and delamination [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The damage modes evidence also supports that milling can produce fibrillation, delamination, and fiber breakage, with hammer-like processes being especially prone to breakage [N6-R3][N6-R4]. So, hammer milling can achieve a finer particle size distribution, but at the cost of more damage and less uniformity.

The energy trade-off is also important. The comparison evidence notes that fine and/or ultrafine milling processes such as ball milling, vibratory ball milling, and centrifugal milling are simpler saccharification technologies that do not require chemical or water inputs and minimize waste generation [N5-F1].
